citeAs: Dan Hendrycks, Collin Burns, Saurav Kadavath, Akul Arora, Steven Basart, Eric Tang, Dawn Song, Jacob Steinhardt (2021). Measuring Mathematical Problem Solving With the MATH Dataset. NeurIPS 2021 Track on Datasets and Benchmarks.
creator: Dan Hendrycks, Collin Burns, Saurav Kadavath, Akul Arora, Steven Basart, Eric Tang, Dawn Song, Jacob Steinhardt (UC Berkeley)
description: MATH (Mathematics Aptitude Test of Heuristics) is a dataset of 12,500 challenging competition mathematics problems (7,500 training and 5,000 test) sourced from high school math competitions including AMC 10, AMC 12, and AIME. Each problem includes a full step-by-step solution written in LaTeX and natural language, and is tagged by subject (7 subjects) and difficulty level (1–5). The dataset is designed to measure mathematical problem-solving ability in machine learning models.
name: MATH
rai:annotatorDemographics: For human evaluation, six university students studying computer science participated. Four participants are authors on the paper. The other two are friends or acquaintances of the authors. All participants gave consent. Participants ranged from those who do not like mathematics (40% accuracy) to a three-time IMO gold medalist (90% accuracy).
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: No crowdsourcing platform was used. The authors note that because MATH requires a strong mathematical background and long time to solve problems, they were restricted to assessing six human participants and could not rely on crowdsourcing sites such as Amazon Mechanical Turk.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Each problem was tagged by subject (one of seven: Prealgebra, Algebra, Number Theory, Counting and Probability, Geometry, Intermediate Algebra, Precalculus) and difficulty level (1–5), following the AoPS difficulty scale. Difficulty level 1 corresponds to the easiest problems (e.g., first problems of AMC 8), while level 5 corresponds to the hardest (e.g., AIME problems). Each problem includes a full step-by-step solution and a final boxed answer.
rai:dataCollection: Problems were collected from mathematics competitions including the AMC 10, AMC 12, AIME, and more. Many problems were collected from aops.com/community/c3158_usa_contests. These competitions span decades and assess the mathematical problem-solving ability of the best young mathematical talent in the United States.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Competition mathematics problems from AMC 10, AMC 12, AIME, and other contests, sourced from aops.com. Problems and solutions are formatted in LaTeX and the Asymptote vector graphics language.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is challenging even for humans: a computer science PhD student attained approximately 40% accuracy, and a three-time IMO gold medalist attained 90%. Models achieve only 3.0%–6.9% accuracy, indicating the benchmark is very hard. The dataset covers only competition mathematics problems from US contests, which may not represent all mathematical problem-solving contexts. The authors note that simply scaling Transformer models is not sufficient to solve MATH.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Problems and solutions were consistently formatted using LaTeX and the Asymptote vector graphics language. Final boxed answers follow strict formatting rules: probabilities expressed as simplified fractions; matrix entry fractions encoded with x/y; other fractions with \frac{x}{y}; coefficients without multiplication symbol; expressions with multiple variables in alphabetical order; polynomials in decreasing degree order. Equivalent representations (e.g., \frac{x}{y} and \dfrac{x}{y}, \left( and (, 0.5 and 1/2) are treated as equivalent during evaluation.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The authors note that even 40% accuracy for a machine learning model would be impressive but would have ramifications for cheating on homework. They explicitly state they do not intend for the dataset to train models that help students cheat on mathematics exams. The dataset is intended to advance mathematical reasoning capabilities in AI, which has broad scientific and intellectual significance given the wide applicability of mathematics.
rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking mathematical problem-solving ability of machine learning models; training models to generate step-by-step answer derivations and explanations; forecasting reasoning capabilities of ML models. The authors explicitly state they do not intend for the dataset to train models that help students cheat on mathematics exams.

null_reasons.rai:annotationsPerItem: The paper does not specify a number of independent annotations per problem; difficulty and subject labels follow AoPS conventions, not a multi-annotator scheme.
null_reasons.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: No inter-annotator agreement metrics or annotation quality analysis are described for the dataset labels.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: The paper does not specify a timeframe for when the competition problems were collected, only noting the competitions span decades.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The paper does not discuss missing data handling for the MATH dataset.
null_reasons.rai:dataImputationProtocol: No imputation protocol is described for the MATH dataset.
null_reasons.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: No post-collection manipulation (augmentation, balancing, resampling) is described for the MATH dataset itself.
null_reasons.rai:machineAnnotationTools: No machine annotation tools are described as being used in the creation or labeling of the MATH dataset.
null_reasons.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset consists of mathematics competition problems and solutions; no personal or sensitive information is collected.
null_reasons.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: No versioning, update cadence, or maintenance plan is described for the MATH dataset.
null_reasons.rai:dataBiases: The paper does not explicitly acknowledge biases in the MATH dataset or describe design decisions to mitigate specific biases.
